analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans new offshore oil and gas drilling in the Atlantic Ocean off the East Coast.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee or floor vote and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The COAST Anti-Drilling Act would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to permanently bar the Interior Department from leasing any part of the Mid-Atlantic or North Atlantic planning areas — the waters off the East Coast — for oil, gas, or mineral exploration, development, or production [S2][S3]. The goal is to protect Atlantic beaches, coastal tourism, and fishing from the risks of offshore drilling [S3]. It was introduced by Rep. Frank Pallone of New Jersey with 7 cosponsors in March 2009 [S1][S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities along the Atlantic — beach towns, tourism businesses, and commercial and recreational fishing interests — gain statutory protection from oil spills and drilling infrastructure off their shores. Oil spills, seismic exploration, and drilling platforms put those economies and shorelines at risk, and a permanent legal ban removes that risk rather than leaving it to the policy preferences of whoever holds the White House [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Atlantic coastal towns, tourism, and fishing

how_it_helps.text: Adds a permanent prohibition to the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act barring Interior from issuing any lease for exploration, development, or production of oil, gas, or minerals in the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas [S2][S3].
Because the ban is written into statute rather than left to administrative policy, it cannot be reversed by a future administration's leasing plan [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies lose potential access to Atlantic reserves, and the federal government forgoes potential lease revenue. To the extent domestic Atlantic production would have modestly increased supply, consumers could see a negligible effect on energy prices — though Atlantic reserves were never confirmed as commercially significant.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas companies and federal lease revenue

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently removes a potential domestic energy source, which drilling proponents argued would reduce energy supply and federal revenue from leases [S2][S3].
A blanket statutory ban forecloses any case-by-case evaluation of whether specific Atlantic areas could be developed safely, rather than allowing balances to be struck area by area.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the Atlantic coastal states the bill covers, the protection is concrete and permanent, and the forfeited drilling revenue was speculative — no producing Atlantic wells existed. The main honest cost is the forgone energy supply and federal revenue, which are real but modest compared with the economic and environmental exposure of coastal communities to a spill. The bill is narrowly drawn to two planning areas rather than the entire Outer Continental Shelf, which limits its broader energy-supply impact.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and never received a markup or a vote before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on March 24, 2009, with 7 cosponsors [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Natural Resources on the day of introduction [S5].
Six days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it stayed for the remainder of the 111th Congress [S5].
No action, markup, or vote followed; the bill expired on January 3, 2011, with the end of the Congress [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept Atlantic waters available for potential future leasing, since no statutory ban was enacted, while Atlantic coastal communities were left without permanent protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas companies; coastal towns left unprotected

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban Atlantic offshore drilling and sought cosponsors for it.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee without ever scheduling a markup or advancing it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors were House Democrats, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record shows where broader support or opposition stood [S1][S4].

industries.note: The bill would have permanently locked the industry out of leasing in the Mid-Atlantic and North Atlantic planning areas [S2][S3]. Drilling profits from developing those waters while the risk of spills and coastal industrialization falls on nearby communities.

A permanent leasing ban protects beaches, fisheries, and tourism-dependent economies from spill risk and drilling infrastructure [S3]. The bill's title names the protection of tourism as a purpose [S3].
